findings.issue: Source: 'hurled him from the heavenly threshold till he came fainting down to earth'; candidate adds 'half' ('until he fell to earth half fainting'), softening the result.
findings.fix: The father of gods and men pitied Hector and glared at Hera. “I see it, Hera, you mischief-making trickster,” he said. “Your cunning has kept Hector from fighting and has routed his army. I am half inclined to thrash you, and you would be the first to reap the fruits of your scurvy knavery. Do you not remember the time I hung you up? I fastened two anvils to your feet and bound your hands in a golden chain that no one could break, and you dangled in mid-air among the clouds. All the gods of Olympus raged, but they could not get near enough to set you free. Any of them I caught, I seized and hurled from the heavenly threshold until he came fainting down to earth. Even that did not ease my mind of its constant anxiety about noble Heracles. You and Boreas had spitefully carried him off across the seas to Cos, after you had won the tempests over to your scheme. But I rescued him, and in spite of all his mighty labors I brought him back to Argos. I remind you of this so that you will learn to stop your deceit, and see how much you are likely to gain from the embraces you left to come here and trick me.”

findings.issue: Source: 'contrary to the desire of myself, Minerva..., Juno, Mercury, and King Vulcan'; candidate 'against the wishes of me, Athena, driver of the spoil, Hera, Hermes, and King Hephaestus' runs the list together so Athena's epithet and the names blur.
findings.fix: Poseidon answered, “Goddess Iris, what you say is well timed. It is good when a messenger shows such discretion. Even so, it cuts me to the heart when anyone rebukes so angrily one who is his own peer and has equal power. Now, though, I will give way, in spite of my displeasure. And let me tell you something more, and I mean it: if Zeus spares steep Ilium and will not let the Achaeans have the great triumph of sacking it, against the wishes of myself, of Athena, driver of the spoil, of Hera, of Hermes, and of King Hephaestus, then let him understand that he will bring on himself our implacable resentment.”

findings.issue: Source: 'which Vulcan the smith had given Jove'; candidate says Hephaestus 'had made for Zeus', adding that he made it, which the source does not state.
findings.fix: The Trojans came on in a dense body, and Hector strode at their head. Phoebus Apollo walked in front of him, with cloud wrapped around his shoulders. In his hands he carried the terrible aegis, shaggy with fringe, that Hephaestus the smith had given to Zeus to strike terror into men’s hearts. Holding it, Apollo led the Trojans on.

findings.issue: Source 'yet though these were fewer in number, they could not drive them back' leaves 'these' ambiguous; candidate resolves it as the Trojans being fewer. A sensible reading, but a choice.

Butler's source is garbled ('sprang upon Lampus was son of Laomedon'); candidate sensibly reads 'Dolops charged in. Lampus was a son of Laomedon'. Also source 'homed stag' typo at p21 is rendered 'horned' (correct).
